page.title: What Is a Variable in Python?
page.introduction: A Python variable is best understood through the relationship between a name and an object. This technical breakdown examines the terminology, execution model, and important rules behind Python variable assignment.
page.definition: A variable in Python is a name that refers to an object. Assignment binds that name to an object rather than placing a value directly inside a variable container.

explanation.content: Consider the statement x = 10. Python evaluates the expression 10, obtains an integer object representing that value, and then binds the name x to that object.
This distinction between names, objects, and references is fundamental to understanding Python's object model.
The same model also explains reassignment, object identity, mutability, aliasing, and how arguments are passed to functions.

terminology.description: An identifier used by Python code to refer to an object.
A runtime entity in Python that has identity, type, and value.
The relationship through which a name provides access to an object.
The association of a name with an object.
An operation that binds a target name to the result of evaluating an expression.
The identity that distinguishes one object from another during its lifetime.

explanation.content: Python uses a name-binding model. A statement such as x = 10 does not mean that the integer value 10 is physically stored inside a box called x.
Instead, Python evaluates the right-hand side, obtains an object, and establishes a binding between the name x and that object.
Conceptually, the execution can be understood as: evaluate 10 → obtain the integer object → bind the name x to that object.
After the second assignment, the name x is bound to the object representing 20. The name has been rebound; Python has not changed the integer object representing 10 into 20.

points.title: Name binding
points.content: Assignment creates or changes the association between a name and an object.

points.title: Everything is an object
points.content: Integers, strings, lists, functions, classes, and many other runtime entities are represented as Python objects.

points.title: Identity matters
points.content: Every object has an identity that distinguishes it from other objects during its lifetime.

points.title: Reassignment
points.content: A name can be rebound to another object without changing the original object.

points.title: Multiple names
points.content: Multiple names can refer to the same object, which is especially important when working with mutable objects.

points.title: Execution model
points.content: Understanding name binding makes assignment, function arguments, aliasing, and mutability easier to reason about.

page.takeaway: At the technical level, a Python variable is a name bound to an object. Understanding this name–object–binding model is essential for reasoning about assignment, identity, mutability, aliasing, and function argument behavior.
